§ 0

What this lecture covers

We take a 2-link planar robot arm with point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ at the distal end of each link, and derive — from scratch — its kinematics and energies.

The destination is the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, written in terms of the joint angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and their rates $\dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2$. Along the way we'll touch every tool you need: homogeneous transformations, the chain rule on position, the trig identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$, and the usual gravity potential.

This is the setup we will hand to the Euler–Lagrange machinery in Module 3.

Don't skim the algebra in step 4 — the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term is the whole reason this problem is interesting.
Setup

The system on the table

Link lengths $L_1, L_2$; joint angles $\theta_1$ (link 1 from horizontal) and $\theta_2$ (link 2 from link 1); tip masses $m_1, m_2$; gravity $g$ acts in $-y$.

§ 1

Write the transformation matrices for each link

We use 2D homogeneous transformations so rotation and translation live in one matrix. From the base to the tip of link 1:

$$T_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_1 & -\sin\theta_1 & L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ \sin\theta_1 & \cos\theta_1 & L_1\sin\theta_1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

From the base to the tip of link 2 (i.e. the location of $m_2$):

$$T_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) & -\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) & L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) & \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) & L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Notice that the rotation block of $T_2$ uses the sum $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ — link 2's orientation in the world is the cumulative rotation, not just $\theta_2$.

Why homogeneous?

One matrix for rotation and translation

The third row/column lets us compose rotations and translations by simple matrix multiplication — $T_2$ is literally $T_1$ composed with link 2's local transform.

Interactive · pick

Pick the rotation entry for $T_2$

Now you pick the (1,1) entry of $T_2$ yourself. The point is to convince you that link 2's world-frame orientation is the cumulative rotation $\theta_1+\theta_2$, not just $\theta_2$ — and certainly not just $\theta_1$.

§ 2

Read off the tip positions

The right-hand column of each transformation matrix is the position of that link's tip in world coordinates.

For $m_1$ (end of link 1):

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ y_1 &= L_1\sin\theta_1 \end{aligned}$$

For $m_2$ (end of link 2):

$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ y_2 &= L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

This is just forward kinematics — geometry, no dynamics yet.

Interactive · animator

Animated forward kinematics · scrub the joints, watch the tip positions

Now you drag $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ and watch the tip-position formulas update live. The point is to see — not just read — that $x_2$ accumulates a contribution from both links, while $x_1$ depends only on $\theta_1$.

§ 3

Differentiate to get velocities

Apply the chain rule — $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are functions of time, so $\cos\theta_1$ differentiates to $-\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1$, and $\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)$ picks up the factor $(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$.

For $m_1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_1 &= -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 \\ \dot y_1 &= L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 \end{aligned}$$

For $m_2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_2 &= -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 - L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \\ \dot y_2 &= L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$
The $(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$ factor on the second term is the easiest thing to forget — link 2's angular rate in the world frame is the sum of both joint rates.

Interactive · builder

Build $\dot x_2$ term by term

Now you build $\dot x_2$ yourself by dragging chain-rule pieces onto a blank expression. You'll discover the hard way that the second term picks up the factor $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$, not just $\dot\theta_2$ — the single most common slip in this derivation.

§ 4

Square and simplify: $v^2$ for each mass

For $m_1$ the algebra is short — Pythagoras plus $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$:

$$v_1^2 = \dot x_1^2 + \dot y_1^2 = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2(\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1) = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2$$

For $m_2$ the algebra is longer. Square both $\dot x_2$ and $\dot y_2$ and add:

$$\begin{aligned} v_2^2 =\;& L_1^2\sin^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \\ & + 2L_1L_2\sin\theta_1\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \\ & + L_1^2\cos^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \\ & + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_1\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

Now collapse using two identities:

  • $\sin^2\alpha + \cos^2\alpha = 1$
  • $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$

with $\alpha = \theta_1$ and $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$, so $\alpha - \beta = -\theta_2$ and $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$:

$$\boxed{\,v_2^2 = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)\,}$$
That $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term is the coupling between the two joints — it's what makes a 2-link arm a genuinely nonlinear system.
Identity in play

Keep this on the tip of your tongue

$\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$. It shows up every time you square the velocity of a multi-link chain.

Interactive · derive

Collapse the cross terms · derive the $\cos\theta_2$ coupling

Now you derive the boxed result for $v_2^2$ yourself by choosing which identity to apply at each step. The four cross-products in the expansion collapse into a single $\cos\theta_2$ term — and you'll see exactly which trig identity makes that happen.

§ 5

Assemble the kinetic energy $T$

With both squared speeds in hand, kinetic energy is just $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2$:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

The shape to notice: $T$ is quadratic in the joint rates $\dot\theta_i$, with coefficients that depend on $\theta_2$ alone (not $\theta_1$). That's a hint of the inertia matrix $M(q)$ — but we'll meet that properly in Module 3.

Looking ahead

The manipulator form is hiding in here

Group the $\dot\theta_i\dot\theta_j$ coefficients and you'll have $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot q^\top M(q)\,\dot q$ — the standard manipulator form.

Interactive · animator

Animated coupling · watch $\cos\theta_2$ shape the kinetic energy

Now you scrub $\theta_2$ and watch the three contributions to $T$ (the pure-$\dot\theta_1$ piece, the pure-$(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$ piece, and the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term) shrink, swap, and vanish. The point is to feel where the coupling matters and where it disappears.

§ 6

Potential energy $V$

With $y$ increasing upward and gravity $g$ acting in $-y$, each mass contributes $m_i g y_i$:

$$V = m_1 g y_1 + m_2 g y_2$$

Substitute the tip-position formulas from step 2:

$$V = m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1 + m_2 g \left[ L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \right]$$

Notice $V$ depends only on the configuration $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ — never on the rates. That's a defining feature of conservative potentials.

§ 7

The Lagrangian $L = T - V$

Stitching it together:

$$L = T - V$$ $$\begin{aligned} L =\;& \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 \\ & + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \, \dot\theta_1 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2) \right] \\ & - m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1 - m_2 g \left[ L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) \right] \end{aligned}$$

This is the object Module 3 will plug into the Euler–Lagrange equations:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\theta_i} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_i} = \tau_i$$

to produce the equations of motion. Everything you need is now on this page.

Save this expression — you'll spend the next lecture differentiating it.
What you just did

Seven steps, one Lagrangian

Geometry → kinematics → velocities → energies → Lagrangian. That is the entire setup phase of analytic robot dynamics, in seven steps.

Interactive · multiple choice

Self-check · what the Lagrangian is telling you

Now you check your understanding of the four most slippery features of this Lagrangian — the $\cos\theta_2$ coupling, the dependence of $V$ on configuration only, the absence of $\theta_1$ from $T$, and the geometric meaning of $\theta_2 = \pi/2$.

Glossary · take stock

Concepts in play today

  • homogeneous transformation matrix
  • forward kinematics
  • chain rule for velocities
  • tip-mass model
  • kinetic energy of a multi-link chain
  • gravitational potential energy
  • Lagrangian $L = T - V$
  • trig identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$
  • coupling term $\cos\theta_2$ between joints
  • preparation for Euler–Lagrange equations

Formative practice

Practice — try these on your own

Small activities to test your grip on today's ideas. Try each one first, then reveal the worked solution to compare.

1 · Sanity-check the single-link case

Set $m_2 = 0$ and $L_2 = 0$ in the 2-link result. What do $T$, $V$, and $L$ collapse to? Verify by hand that this matches what you would have written for a single point mass $m_1$ on a massless rod of length $L_1$ pinned at the origin.

Self-check after you've tried

Your $T$ should be $\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$ · your $V$ should be $m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1$ · the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term should vanish entirely.

Show worked solution

Substitute $m_2 = 0$ into

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \, \dot\theta_1 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2) \right]$$

The entire bracketed term vanishes, leaving $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$.

For the potential energy, $m_2 = 0$ kills the second contribution:

$$V = m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1$$

So the Lagrangian collapses to

$$\boxed{\,L = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 - m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1\,}$$

This is exactly the Lagrangian of a simple pendulum of length $L_1$ and bob mass $m_1$, measured from the horizontal (so the gravitational term carries $\sin\theta_1$ rather than the more familiar $-\cos\theta_1$ — that's just a choice of zero, not a different physical system). Good — the 2-link formula reduces cleanly to the 1-link case, which is the basic consistency check every multi-body derivation must pass.

2 · Derive the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term yourself

Without peeking at step 4 of the lecture, start from

$$\dot x_2 = -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 - L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$$ $$\dot y_2 = L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$$

and derive $v_2^2 = \dot x_2^2 + \dot y_2^2$. Show explicitly which trig identity collapses the four cross-products into the single term $2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$.

Self-check after you've tried

After squaring you should see four cross-product terms (two from $\dot x_2^2$, two from $\dot y_2^2$) · the $\sin\sin$ and $\cos\cos$ cross-products should combine via $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$ · with $\alpha = \theta_1$ and $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$ the result is $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$.

Show worked solution

Square each component. Using $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$:

$$\dot x_2^2 = L_1^2 \sin^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \sin\theta_1 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) + L_2^2 \sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$$ $$\dot y_2^2 = L_1^2 \cos^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_1 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) + L_2^2 \cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$$

Add them and group by structure:

Pure $\dot\theta_1^2$ terms: $L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 (\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1) = L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$.

Pure $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$ terms: $L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 (\sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)) = L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$.

Cross terms:

$$2 L_1 L_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \Big[ \sin\theta_1 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \cos\theta_1 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \Big]$$

The bracket is exactly $\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$ with $\alpha = \theta_1$, $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$, so $\alpha - \beta = -\theta_2$ and $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$.

Putting it together:

$$\boxed{\,v_2^2 = L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)\,}$$

The identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$ is what packages the geometry into a single, configuration-dependent coupling coefficient.

3 · Evaluate $T$ at a stretched-out configuration

Compute the kinetic energy $T$ for the arm at the instant when $\theta_2 = 0$ (link 2 perfectly aligned with link 1, arm fully extended), with both joints rotating at the same rate $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$. Simplify as far as you can in terms of $m_1, m_2, L_1, L_2, \omega$.

Self-check after you've tried

At $\theta_2 = 0$, $\cos\theta_2 = 1$ · with $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$, the factor $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) = 2\omega$ · all $\theta_1$ dependence should drop out of $T$ (kinetic energy doesn't care where $\theta_1$ points, only how fast it's changing).

Show worked solution

Substitute $\theta_2 = 0$ and $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$ into

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

Replace term by term:

  • $\dot\theta_1^2 \to \omega^2$
  • $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \to (2\omega)^2 = 4\omega^2$
  • $\cos\theta_2 \to 1$
  • $\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \to \omega \cdot 2\omega = 2\omega^2$

The $m_2$ bracket becomes:

$$L_1^2 \omega^2 + 4 L_2^2 \omega^2 + 4 L_1 L_2 \omega^2 = \omega^2 \left( L_1^2 + 4 L_1 L_2 + 4 L_2^2 \right) = \omega^2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2$$

So

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \omega^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \omega^2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2$$ $$\boxed{\,T = \tfrac{1}{2} \omega^2 \left[ m_1 L_1^2 + m_2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2 \right]\,}$$

Geometric sanity check: when the arm is fully extended ($\theta_2 = 0$) and both joints spin together at $\omega$, the world-frame angular rate of link 2 is $\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2 = 2\omega$. The mass $m_2$ sits at distance $L_1 + L_2$ from the base, but its speed has separate contributions $L_1\omega$ (from joint 1's rotation) and $2 L_2 \omega$ (from link 2's world-frame angular rate $2\omega$ applied at its own length $L_2$), and because the arm is stretched out these add coherently. The clean algebraic statement is $v_2 = (L_1 + 2L_2)\omega$ at this instant, which matches the squared form.

4 · Identify the inertia-matrix entries

Manipulator dynamics is usually written $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot q^\top M(q)\,\dot q$ with $q = (\theta_1, \theta_2)^\top$. By grouping coefficients of $\dot\theta_1^2$, $\dot\theta_2^2$, and $\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2$ in the kinetic energy from step 5, read off the entries $M_{11}, M_{12} = M_{21}, M_{22}$ of the symmetric inertia matrix.

Self-check after you've tried

$M$ should be $2\times 2$ and symmetric · the only configuration variable appearing in $M$ should be $\theta_2$ (never $\theta_1$, by rotational symmetry of the base joint) · only the $L_1 L_2$ piece of $M_{12}$ should vanish when $\cos\theta_2 = 0$; the $m_2 L_2^2$ piece survives because it comes from link 2's own rotation.

Show worked solution

Expand the kinetic energy fully so every coefficient of $\dot\theta_i \dot\theta_j$ is visible. Starting from

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

expand the inner pieces:

  • $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 = \dot\theta_1^2 + 2\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2 + \dot\theta_2^2$
  • $\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) = \dot\theta_1^2 + \dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2$

Substitute and collect:

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_1^2$:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2$$

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_2^2$:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2$$

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_1 \dot\theta_2$:

$$m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2$$

Now match against $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\left( M_{11}\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 M_{12}\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2 + M_{22}\dot\theta_2^2 \right)$. The factor of 2 on the cross-term is what makes the matrix symmetric:

$$\boxed{\,M_{11} = m_1 L_1^2 + m_2 L_1^2 + m_2 L_2^2 + 2 m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\,}$$ $$\boxed{\,M_{12} = M_{21} = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\,}$$ $$\boxed{\,M_{22} = m_2 L_2^2\,}$$

Self-check verified: $M$ is symmetric; only $\theta_2$ appears (not $\theta_1$, as expected by symmetry); and at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, $\cos\theta_2 = 0$, so $M_{12} = m_2 L_2^2$ — only the $L_1 L_2$ part of the cross-term vanishes; the $m_2 L_2^2$ piece survives because it comes from link 2's own rotation, which is geometry-independent. The cleanest decoupling is at the limit $L_1 \to 0$, not at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$. This is exactly the inertia matrix you will see again in Module 3, and it is the launchpad for writing Coriolis and centrifugal terms via the Christoffel symbols of $M(q)$.

The deepest reason for this is:`, options: [ String.raw`We placed the base joint at the origin of world coordinates, which algebraically removes $\theta_1$ from the expression`, String.raw`Gravity has already been subtracted off when we wrote $T$, which would otherwise have reintroduced a $\theta_1$ dependence`, String.raw`The $\theta_1$ dependence cancels purely through the $\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1 = 1$ identity applied in step 4`, String.raw`Kinetic energy is invariant under rigid rotation of the entire arm about the base joint, so $\theta_1$ cannot appear` ], correct: 3, explain: String.raw`It's a symmetry argument: rotating the entire arm about its base changes $\theta_1$ but leaves all velocity magnitudes (and therefore $T$) unchanged. Lecture 03 · Module 2 · Robotics

Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm

From transformation matrices to the Lagrangian — a fully worked tip-mass derivation.

Today we walk through, step by careful step, how a 2-link planar arm with tip masses goes from geometry to Lagrangian. We start with homogeneous transformation matrices, read off the tip positions, differentiate to get velocities, square them, and stitch everything together into kinetic and potential energy.

By the end you will have $L = T - V$ written out explicitly — exactly the form Module 3 will need when we feed it into the Euler–Lagrange equations.

Contents

§ 0

What this lecture covers

We take a 2-link planar robot arm with point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ at the distal end of each link, and derive — from scratch — its kinematics and energies.

The destination is the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, written in terms of the joint angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and their rates $\dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2$. Along the way we'll touch every tool you need: homogeneous transformations, the chain rule on position, the trig identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$, and the usual gravity potential.

This is the setup we will hand to the Euler–Lagrange machinery in Module 3.

Don't skim the algebra in step 4 — the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term is the whole reason this problem is interesting.
Setup

The system on the table

Link lengths $L_1, L_2$; joint angles $\theta_1$ (link 1 from horizontal) and $\theta_2$ (link 2 from link 1); tip masses $m_1, m_2$; gravity $g$ acts in $-y$.

§ 1

Write the transformation matrices for each link

We use 2D homogeneous transformations so rotation and translation live in one matrix. From the base to the tip of link 1:

$$T_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_1 & -\sin\theta_1 & L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ \sin\theta_1 & \cos\theta_1 & L_1\sin\theta_1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

From the base to the tip of link 2 (i.e. the location of $m_2$):

$$T_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) & -\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) & L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) & \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) & L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Notice that the rotation block of $T_2$ uses the sum $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ — link 2's orientation in the world is the cumulative rotation, not just $\theta_2$.

Why homogeneous?

One matrix for rotation and translation

The third row/column lets us compose rotations and translations by simple matrix multiplication — $T_2$ is literally $T_1$ composed with link 2's local transform.

Interactive · pick

Pick the rotation entry for $T_2$

Now you pick the (1,1) entry of $T_2$ yourself. The point is to convince you that link 2's world-frame orientation is the cumulative rotation $\theta_1+\theta_2$, not just $\theta_2$ — and certainly not just $\theta_1$.

§ 2

Read off the tip positions

The right-hand column of each transformation matrix is the position of that link's tip in world coordinates.

For $m_1$ (end of link 1):

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ y_1 &= L_1\sin\theta_1 \end{aligned}$$

For $m_2$ (end of link 2):

$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ y_2 &= L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

This is just forward kinematics — geometry, no dynamics yet.

Interactive · animator

Animated forward kinematics · scrub the joints, watch the tip positions

Now you drag $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ and watch the tip-position formulas update live. The point is to see — not just read — that $x_2$ accumulates a contribution from both links, while $x_1$ depends only on $\theta_1$.

§ 3

Differentiate to get velocities

Apply the chain rule — $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are functions of time, so $\cos\theta_1$ differentiates to $-\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1$, and $\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)$ picks up the factor $(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$.

For $m_1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_1 &= -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 \\ \dot y_1 &= L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 \end{aligned}$$

For $m_2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_2 &= -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 - L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \\ \dot y_2 &= L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$
The $(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$ factor on the second term is the easiest thing to forget — link 2's angular rate in the world frame is the sum of both joint rates.

Interactive · builder

Build $\dot x_2$ term by term

Now you build $\dot x_2$ yourself by dragging chain-rule pieces onto a blank expression. You'll discover the hard way that the second term picks up the factor $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$, not just $\dot\theta_2$ — the single most common slip in this derivation.

§ 4

Square and simplify: $v^2$ for each mass

For $m_1$ the algebra is short — Pythagoras plus $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$:

$$v_1^2 = \dot x_1^2 + \dot y_1^2 = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2(\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1) = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2$$

For $m_2$ the algebra is longer. Square both $\dot x_2$ and $\dot y_2$ and add:

$$\begin{aligned} v_2^2 =\;& L_1^2\sin^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \\ & + 2L_1L_2\sin\theta_1\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \\ & + L_1^2\cos^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \\ & + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_1\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

Now collapse using two identities:

  • $\sin^2\alpha + \cos^2\alpha = 1$
  • $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$

with $\alpha = \theta_1$ and $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$, so $\alpha - \beta = -\theta_2$ and $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$:

$$\boxed{\,v_2^2 = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)\,}$$
That $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term is the coupling between the two joints — it's what makes a 2-link arm a genuinely nonlinear system.
Identity in play

Keep this on the tip of your tongue

$\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$. It shows up every time you square the velocity of a multi-link chain.

Interactive · derive

Collapse the cross terms · derive the $\cos\theta_2$ coupling

Now you derive the boxed result for $v_2^2$ yourself by choosing which identity to apply at each step. The four cross-products in the expansion collapse into a single $\cos\theta_2$ term — and you'll see exactly which trig identity makes that happen.

§ 5

Assemble the kinetic energy $T$

With both squared speeds in hand, kinetic energy is just $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2$:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

The shape to notice: $T$ is quadratic in the joint rates $\dot\theta_i$, with coefficients that depend on $\theta_2$ alone (not $\theta_1$). That's a hint of the inertia matrix $M(q)$ — but we'll meet that properly in Module 3.

Looking ahead

The manipulator form is hiding in here

Group the $\dot\theta_i\dot\theta_j$ coefficients and you'll have $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot q^\top M(q)\,\dot q$ — the standard manipulator form.

Interactive · animator

Animated coupling · watch $\cos\theta_2$ shape the kinetic energy

Now you scrub $\theta_2$ and watch the three contributions to $T$ (the pure-$\dot\theta_1$ piece, the pure-$(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$ piece, and the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term) shrink, swap, and vanish. The point is to feel where the coupling matters and where it disappears.

§ 6

Potential energy $V$

With $y$ increasing upward and gravity $g$ acting in $-y$, each mass contributes $m_i g y_i$:

$$V = m_1 g y_1 + m_2 g y_2$$

Substitute the tip-position formulas from step 2:

$$V = m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1 + m_2 g \left[ L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \right]$$

Notice $V$ depends only on the configuration $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ — never on the rates. That's a defining feature of conservative potentials.

§ 7

The Lagrangian $L = T - V$

Stitching it together:

$$L = T - V$$ $$\begin{aligned} L =\;& \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 \\ & + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \, \dot\theta_1 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2) \right] \\ & - m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1 - m_2 g \left[ L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) \right] \end{aligned}$$

This is the object Module 3 will plug into the Euler–Lagrange equations:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\theta_i} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_i} = \tau_i$$

to produce the equations of motion. Everything you need is now on this page.

Save this expression — you'll spend the next lecture differentiating it.
What you just did

Seven steps, one Lagrangian

Geometry → kinematics → velocities → energies → Lagrangian. That is the entire setup phase of analytic robot dynamics, in seven steps.

Interactive · multiple choice

Self-check · what the Lagrangian is telling you

Now you check your understanding of the four most slippery features of this Lagrangian — the $\cos\theta_2$ coupling, the dependence of $V$ on configuration only, the absence of $\theta_1$ from $T$, and the geometric meaning of $\theta_2 = \pi/2$.

Glossary · take stock

Concepts in play today

  • homogeneous transformation matrix
  • forward kinematics
  • chain rule for velocities
  • tip-mass model
  • kinetic energy of a multi-link chain
  • gravitational potential energy
  • Lagrangian $L = T - V$
  • trig identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$
  • coupling term $\cos\theta_2$ between joints
  • preparation for Euler–Lagrange equations

Formative practice

Practice — try these on your own

Small activities to test your grip on today's ideas. Try each one first, then reveal the worked solution to compare.

1 · Sanity-check the single-link case

Set $m_2 = 0$ and $L_2 = 0$ in the 2-link result. What do $T$, $V$, and $L$ collapse to? Verify by hand that this matches what you would have written for a single point mass $m_1$ on a massless rod of length $L_1$ pinned at the origin.

Self-check after you've tried

Your $T$ should be $\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$ · your $V$ should be $m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1$ · the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term should vanish entirely.

Show worked solution

Substitute $m_2 = 0$ into

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \, \dot\theta_1 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2) \right]$$

The entire bracketed term vanishes, leaving $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$.

For the potential energy, $m_2 = 0$ kills the second contribution:

$$V = m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1$$

So the Lagrangian collapses to

$$\boxed{\,L = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 - m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1\,}$$

This is exactly the Lagrangian of a simple pendulum of length $L_1$ and bob mass $m_1$, measured from the horizontal (so the gravitational term carries $\sin\theta_1$ rather than the more familiar $-\cos\theta_1$ — that's just a choice of zero, not a different physical system). Good — the 2-link formula reduces cleanly to the 1-link case, which is the basic consistency check every multi-body derivation must pass.

2 · Derive the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term yourself

Without peeking at step 4 of the lecture, start from

$$\dot x_2 = -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 - L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$$ $$\dot y_2 = L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$$

and derive $v_2^2 = \dot x_2^2 + \dot y_2^2$. Show explicitly which trig identity collapses the four cross-products into the single term $2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$.

Self-check after you've tried

After squaring you should see four cross-product terms (two from $\dot x_2^2$, two from $\dot y_2^2$) · the $\sin\sin$ and $\cos\cos$ cross-products should combine via $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$ · with $\alpha = \theta_1$ and $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$ the result is $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$.

Show worked solution

Square each component. Using $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$:

$$\dot x_2^2 = L_1^2 \sin^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \sin\theta_1 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) + L_2^2 \sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$$ $$\dot y_2^2 = L_1^2 \cos^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_1 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) + L_2^2 \cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$$

Add them and group by structure:

Pure $\dot\theta_1^2$ terms: $L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 (\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1) = L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$.

Pure $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$ terms: $L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 (\sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)) = L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$.

Cross terms:

$$2 L_1 L_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \Big[ \sin\theta_1 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \cos\theta_1 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \Big]$$

The bracket is exactly $\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$ with $\alpha = \theta_1$, $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$, so $\alpha - \beta = -\theta_2$ and $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$.

Putting it together:

$$\boxed{\,v_2^2 = L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)\,}$$

The identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$ is what packages the geometry into a single, configuration-dependent coupling coefficient.

3 · Evaluate $T$ at a stretched-out configuration

Compute the kinetic energy $T$ for the arm at the instant when $\theta_2 = 0$ (link 2 perfectly aligned with link 1, arm fully extended), with both joints rotating at the same rate $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$. Simplify as far as you can in terms of $m_1, m_2, L_1, L_2, \omega$.

Self-check after you've tried

At $\theta_2 = 0$, $\cos\theta_2 = 1$ · with $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$, the factor $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) = 2\omega$ · all $\theta_1$ dependence should drop out of $T$ (kinetic energy doesn't care where $\theta_1$ points, only how fast it's changing).

Show worked solution

Substitute $\theta_2 = 0$ and $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$ into

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

Replace term by term:

  • $\dot\theta_1^2 \to \omega^2$
  • $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \to (2\omega)^2 = 4\omega^2$
  • $\cos\theta_2 \to 1$
  • $\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \to \omega \cdot 2\omega = 2\omega^2$

The $m_2$ bracket becomes:

$$L_1^2 \omega^2 + 4 L_2^2 \omega^2 + 4 L_1 L_2 \omega^2 = \omega^2 \left( L_1^2 + 4 L_1 L_2 + 4 L_2^2 \right) = \omega^2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2$$

So

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \omega^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \omega^2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2$$ $$\boxed{\,T = \tfrac{1}{2} \omega^2 \left[ m_1 L_1^2 + m_2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2 \right]\,}$$

Geometric sanity check: when the arm is fully extended ($\theta_2 = 0$) and both joints spin together at $\omega$, the world-frame angular rate of link 2 is $\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2 = 2\omega$. The mass $m_2$ sits at distance $L_1 + L_2$ from the base, but its speed has separate contributions $L_1\omega$ (from joint 1's rotation) and $2 L_2 \omega$ (from link 2's world-frame angular rate $2\omega$ applied at its own length $L_2$), and because the arm is stretched out these add coherently. The clean algebraic statement is $v_2 = (L_1 + 2L_2)\omega$ at this instant, which matches the squared form.

4 · Identify the inertia-matrix entries

Manipulator dynamics is usually written $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot q^\top M(q)\,\dot q$ with $q = (\theta_1, \theta_2)^\top$. By grouping coefficients of $\dot\theta_1^2$, $\dot\theta_2^2$, and $\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2$ in the kinetic energy from step 5, read off the entries $M_{11}, M_{12} = M_{21}, M_{22}$ of the symmetric inertia matrix.

Self-check after you've tried

$M$ should be $2\times 2$ and symmetric · the only configuration variable appearing in $M$ should be $\theta_2$ (never $\theta_1$, by rotational symmetry of the base joint) · only the $L_1 L_2$ piece of $M_{12}$ should vanish when $\cos\theta_2 = 0$; the $m_2 L_2^2$ piece survives because it comes from link 2's own rotation.

Show worked solution

Expand the kinetic energy fully so every coefficient of $\dot\theta_i \dot\theta_j$ is visible. Starting from

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

expand the inner pieces:

  • $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 = \dot\theta_1^2 + 2\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2 + \dot\theta_2^2$
  • $\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) = \dot\theta_1^2 + \dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2$

Substitute and collect:

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_1^2$:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2$$

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_2^2$:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2$$

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_1 \dot\theta_2$:

$$m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2$$

Now match against $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\left( M_{11}\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 M_{12}\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2 + M_{22}\dot\theta_2^2 \right)$. The factor of 2 on the cross-term is what makes the matrix symmetric:

$$\boxed{\,M_{11} = m_1 L_1^2 + m_2 L_1^2 + m_2 L_2^2 + 2 m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\,}$$ $$\boxed{\,M_{12} = M_{21} = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\,}$$ $$\boxed{\,M_{22} = m_2 L_2^2\,}$$

Self-check verified: $M$ is symmetric; only $\theta_2$ appears (not $\theta_1$, as expected by symmetry); and at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, $\cos\theta_2 = 0$, so $M_{12} = m_2 L_2^2$ — only the $L_1 L_2$ part of the cross-term vanishes; the $m_2 L_2^2$ piece survives because it comes from link 2's own rotation, which is geometry-independent. The cleanest decoupling is at the limit $L_1 \to 0$, not at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$. This is exactly the inertia matrix you will see again in Module 3, and it is the launchpad for writing Coriolis and centrifugal terms via the Christoffel symbols of $M(q)$.

Lecture 03 · Module 2 · Robotics

Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm

From transformation matrices to the Lagrangian — a fully worked tip-mass derivation.

Today we walk through, step by careful step, how a 2-link planar arm with tip masses goes from geometry to Lagrangian. We start with homogeneous transformation matrices, read off the tip positions, differentiate to get velocities, square them, and stitch everything together into kinetic and potential energy.

By the end you will have $L = T - V$ written out explicitly — exactly the form Module 3 will need when we feed it into the Euler–Lagrange equations.

Contents

§ 0

What this lecture covers

We take a 2-link planar robot arm with point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ at the distal end of each link, and derive — from scratch — its kinematics and energies.

The destination is the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, written in terms of the joint angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and their rates $\dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2$. Along the way we'll touch every tool you need: homogeneous transformations, the chain rule on position, the trig identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$, and the usual gravity potential.

This is the setup we will hand to the Euler–Lagrange machinery in Module 3.

Don't skim the algebra in step 4 — the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term is the whole reason this problem is interesting.
Setup

The system on the table

Link lengths $L_1, L_2$; joint angles $\theta_1$ (link 1 from horizontal) and $\theta_2$ (link 2 from link 1); tip masses $m_1, m_2$; gravity $g$ acts in $-y$.

§ 1

Write the transformation matrices for each link

We use 2D homogeneous transformations so rotation and translation live in one matrix. From the base to the tip of link 1:

$$T_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_1 & -\sin\theta_1 & L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ \sin\theta_1 & \cos\theta_1 & L_1\sin\theta_1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

From the base to the tip of link 2 (i.e. the location of $m_2$):

$$T_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) & -\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) & L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) & \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) & L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Notice that the rotation block of $T_2$ uses the sum $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ — link 2's orientation in the world is the cumulative rotation, not just $\theta_2$.

Why homogeneous?

One matrix for rotation and translation

The third row/column lets us compose rotations and translations by simple matrix multiplication — $T_2$ is literally $T_1$ composed with link 2's local transform.

Interactive · pick

Pick the rotation entry for $T_2$

Now you pick the (1,1) entry of $T_2$ yourself. The point is to convince you that link 2's world-frame orientation is the cumulative rotation $\theta_1+\theta_2$, not just $\theta_2$ — and certainly not just $\theta_1$.

§ 2

Read off the tip positions

The right-hand column of each transformation matrix is the position of that link's tip in world coordinates.

For $m_1$ (end of link 1):

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ y_1 &= L_1\sin\theta_1 \end{aligned}$$

For $m_2$ (end of link 2):

$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ y_2 &= L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

This is just forward kinematics — geometry, no dynamics yet.

Interactive · animator

Animated forward kinematics · scrub the joints, watch the tip positions

Now you drag $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ and watch the tip-position formulas update live. The point is to see — not just read — that $x_2$ accumulates a contribution from both links, while $x_1$ depends only on $\theta_1$.

§ 3

Differentiate to get velocities

Apply the chain rule — $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are functions of time, so $\cos\theta_1$ differentiates to $-\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1$, and $\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)$ picks up the factor $(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$.

For $m_1$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_1 &= -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 \\ \dot y_1 &= L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 \end{aligned}$$

For $m_2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x_2 &= -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 - L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \\ \dot y_2 &= L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$
The $(\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)$ factor on the second term is the easiest thing to forget — link 2's angular rate in the world frame is the sum of both joint rates.

Interactive · builder

Build $\dot x_2$ term by term

Now you build $\dot x_2$ yourself by dragging chain-rule pieces onto a blank expression. You'll discover the hard way that the second term picks up the factor $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$, not just $\dot\theta_2$ — the single most common slip in this derivation.

§ 4

Square and simplify: $v^2$ for each mass

For $m_1$ the algebra is short — Pythagoras plus $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$:

$$v_1^2 = \dot x_1^2 + \dot y_1^2 = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2(\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1) = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2$$

For $m_2$ the algebra is longer. Square both $\dot x_2$ and $\dot y_2$ and add:

$$\begin{aligned} v_2^2 =\;& L_1^2\sin^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \\ & + 2L_1L_2\sin\theta_1\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \\ & + L_1^2\cos^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \\ & + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_1\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$

Now collapse using two identities:

  • $\sin^2\alpha + \cos^2\alpha = 1$
  • $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$

with $\alpha = \theta_1$ and $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$, so $\alpha - \beta = -\theta_2$ and $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$:

$$\boxed{\,v_2^2 = L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)\,}$$
That $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term is the coupling between the two joints — it's what makes a 2-link arm a genuinely nonlinear system.
Identity in play

Keep this on the tip of your tongue

$\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$. It shows up every time you square the velocity of a multi-link chain.

Interactive · derive

Collapse the cross terms · derive the $\cos\theta_2$ coupling

Now you derive the boxed result for $v_2^2$ yourself by choosing which identity to apply at each step. The four cross-products in the expansion collapse into a single $\cos\theta_2$ term — and you'll see exactly which trig identity makes that happen.

§ 5

Assemble the kinetic energy $T$

With both squared speeds in hand, kinetic energy is just $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2$:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2\dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\theta_2\,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

The shape to notice: $T$ is quadratic in the joint rates $\dot\theta_i$, with coefficients that depend on $\theta_2$ alone (not $\theta_1$). That's a hint of the inertia matrix $M(q)$ — but we'll meet that properly in Module 3.

Looking ahead

The manipulator form is hiding in here

Group the $\dot\theta_i\dot\theta_j$ coefficients and you'll have $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot q^\top M(q)\,\dot q$ — the standard manipulator form.

Interactive · animator

Animated coupling · watch $\cos\theta_2$ shape the kinetic energy

Now you scrub $\theta_2$ and watch the three contributions to $T$ (the pure-$\dot\theta_1$ piece, the pure-$(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$ piece, and the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term) shrink, swap, and vanish. The point is to feel where the coupling matters and where it disappears.

§ 6

Potential energy $V$

With $y$ increasing upward and gravity $g$ acting in $-y$, each mass contributes $m_i g y_i$:

$$V = m_1 g y_1 + m_2 g y_2$$

Substitute the tip-position formulas from step 2:

$$V = m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1 + m_2 g \left[ L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \right]$$

Notice $V$ depends only on the configuration $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ — never on the rates. That's a defining feature of conservative potentials.

§ 7

The Lagrangian $L = T - V$

Stitching it together:

$$L = T - V$$ $$\begin{aligned} L =\;& \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 \\ & + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \, \dot\theta_1 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2) \right] \\ & - m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1 - m_2 g \left[ L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) \right] \end{aligned}$$

This is the object Module 3 will plug into the Euler–Lagrange equations:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot\theta_i} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_i} = \tau_i$$

to produce the equations of motion. Everything you need is now on this page.

Save this expression — you'll spend the next lecture differentiating it.
What you just did

Seven steps, one Lagrangian

Geometry → kinematics → velocities → energies → Lagrangian. That is the entire setup phase of analytic robot dynamics, in seven steps.

Interactive · multiple choice

Self-check · what the Lagrangian is telling you

Now you check your understanding of the four most slippery features of this Lagrangian — the $\cos\theta_2$ coupling, the dependence of $V$ on configuration only, the absence of $\theta_1$ from $T$, and the geometric meaning of $\theta_2 = \pi/2$.

Glossary · take stock

Concepts in play today

  • homogeneous transformation matrix
  • forward kinematics
  • chain rule for velocities
  • tip-mass model
  • kinetic energy of a multi-link chain
  • gravitational potential energy
  • Lagrangian $L = T - V$
  • trig identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$
  • coupling term $\cos\theta_2$ between joints
  • preparation for Euler–Lagrange equations

Formative practice

Practice — try these on your own

Small activities to test your grip on today's ideas. Try each one first, then reveal the worked solution to compare.

1 · Sanity-check the single-link case

Set $m_2 = 0$ and $L_2 = 0$ in the 2-link result. What do $T$, $V$, and $L$ collapse to? Verify by hand that this matches what you would have written for a single point mass $m_1$ on a massless rod of length $L_1$ pinned at the origin.

Self-check after you've tried

Your $T$ should be $\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$ · your $V$ should be $m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1$ · the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term should vanish entirely.

Show worked solution

Substitute $m_2 = 0$ into

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \, \dot\theta_1 (\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2) \right]$$

The entire bracketed term vanishes, leaving $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$.

For the potential energy, $m_2 = 0$ kills the second contribution:

$$V = m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1$$

So the Lagrangian collapses to

$$\boxed{\,L = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 - m_1 g L_1 \sin\theta_1\,}$$

This is exactly the Lagrangian of a simple pendulum of length $L_1$ and bob mass $m_1$, measured from the horizontal (so the gravitational term carries $\sin\theta_1$ rather than the more familiar $-\cos\theta_1$ — that's just a choice of zero, not a different physical system). Good — the 2-link formula reduces cleanly to the 1-link case, which is the basic consistency check every multi-body derivation must pass.

2 · Derive the $\cos\theta_2$ cross-term yourself

Without peeking at step 4 of the lecture, start from

$$\dot x_2 = -L_1\sin\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 - L_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$$ $$\dot y_2 = L_1\cos\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$$

and derive $v_2^2 = \dot x_2^2 + \dot y_2^2$. Show explicitly which trig identity collapses the four cross-products into the single term $2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)$.

Self-check after you've tried

After squaring you should see four cross-product terms (two from $\dot x_2^2$, two from $\dot y_2^2$) · the $\sin\sin$ and $\cos\cos$ cross-products should combine via $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$ · with $\alpha = \theta_1$ and $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$ the result is $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$.

Show worked solution

Square each component. Using $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$:

$$\dot x_2^2 = L_1^2 \sin^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \sin\theta_1 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) + L_2^2 \sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$$ $$\dot y_2^2 = L_1^2 \cos^2\theta_1\,\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_1 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) + L_2^2 \cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$$

Add them and group by structure:

Pure $\dot\theta_1^2$ terms: $L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 (\sin^2\theta_1 + \cos^2\theta_1) = L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2$.

Pure $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$ terms: $L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 (\sin^2(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \cos^2(\theta_1+\theta_2)) = L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2$.

Cross terms:

$$2 L_1 L_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \Big[ \sin\theta_1 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) + \cos\theta_1 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \Big]$$

The bracket is exactly $\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$ with $\alpha = \theta_1$, $\beta = \theta_1+\theta_2$, so $\alpha - \beta = -\theta_2$ and $\cos(-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_2$.

Putting it together:

$$\boxed{\,v_2^2 = L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)\,}$$

The identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha-\beta)$ is what packages the geometry into a single, configuration-dependent coupling coefficient.

3 · Evaluate $T$ at a stretched-out configuration

Compute the kinetic energy $T$ for the arm at the instant when $\theta_2 = 0$ (link 2 perfectly aligned with link 1, arm fully extended), with both joints rotating at the same rate $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$. Simplify as far as you can in terms of $m_1, m_2, L_1, L_2, \omega$.

Self-check after you've tried

At $\theta_2 = 0$, $\cos\theta_2 = 1$ · with $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$, the factor $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) = 2\omega$ · all $\theta_1$ dependence should drop out of $T$ (kinetic energy doesn't care where $\theta_1$ points, only how fast it's changing).

Show worked solution

Substitute $\theta_2 = 0$ and $\dot\theta_1 = \dot\theta_2 = \omega$ into

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

Replace term by term:

  • $\dot\theta_1^2 \to \omega^2$
  • $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 \to (2\omega)^2 = 4\omega^2$
  • $\cos\theta_2 \to 1$
  • $\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \to \omega \cdot 2\omega = 2\omega^2$

The $m_2$ bracket becomes:

$$L_1^2 \omega^2 + 4 L_2^2 \omega^2 + 4 L_1 L_2 \omega^2 = \omega^2 \left( L_1^2 + 4 L_1 L_2 + 4 L_2^2 \right) = \omega^2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2$$

So

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \omega^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \omega^2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2$$ $$\boxed{\,T = \tfrac{1}{2} \omega^2 \left[ m_1 L_1^2 + m_2 (L_1 + 2L_2)^2 \right]\,}$$

Geometric sanity check: when the arm is fully extended ($\theta_2 = 0$) and both joints spin together at $\omega$, the world-frame angular rate of link 2 is $\dot\theta_1 + \dot\theta_2 = 2\omega$. The mass $m_2$ sits at distance $L_1 + L_2$ from the base, but its speed has separate contributions $L_1\omega$ (from joint 1's rotation) and $2 L_2 \omega$ (from link 2's world-frame angular rate $2\omega$ applied at its own length $L_2$), and because the arm is stretched out these add coherently. The clean algebraic statement is $v_2 = (L_1 + 2L_2)\omega$ at this instant, which matches the squared form.

4 · Identify the inertia-matrix entries

Manipulator dynamics is usually written $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot q^\top M(q)\,\dot q$ with $q = (\theta_1, \theta_2)^\top$. By grouping coefficients of $\dot\theta_1^2$, $\dot\theta_2^2$, and $\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2$ in the kinetic energy from step 5, read off the entries $M_{11}, M_{12} = M_{21}, M_{22}$ of the symmetric inertia matrix.

Self-check after you've tried

$M$ should be $2\times 2$ and symmetric · the only configuration variable appearing in $M$ should be $\theta_2$ (never $\theta_1$, by rotational symmetry of the base joint) · only the $L_1 L_2$ piece of $M_{12}$ should vanish when $\cos\theta_2 = 0$; the $m_2 L_2^2$ piece survives because it comes from link 2's own rotation.

Show worked solution

Expand the kinetic energy fully so every coefficient of $\dot\theta_i \dot\theta_j$ is visible. Starting from

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \left[ L_1^2 \dot\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \,\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) \right]$$

expand the inner pieces:

  • $(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2)^2 = \dot\theta_1^2 + 2\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2 + \dot\theta_2^2$
  • $\dot\theta_1(\dot\theta_1+\dot\theta_2) = \dot\theta_1^2 + \dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2$

Substitute and collect:

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_1^2$:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2$$

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_2^2$:

$$\tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2$$

Coefficient of $\dot\theta_1 \dot\theta_2$:

$$m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2$$

Now match against $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\left( M_{11}\dot\theta_1^2 + 2 M_{12}\dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2 + M_{22}\dot\theta_2^2 \right)$. The factor of 2 on the cross-term is what makes the matrix symmetric:

$$\boxed{\,M_{11} = m_1 L_1^2 + m_2 L_1^2 + m_2 L_2^2 + 2 m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\,}$$ $$\boxed{\,M_{12} = M_{21} = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\,}$$ $$\boxed{\,M_{22} = m_2 L_2^2\,}$$

Self-check verified: $M$ is symmetric; only $\theta_2$ appears (not $\theta_1$, as expected by symmetry); and at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, $\cos\theta_2 = 0$, so $M_{12} = m_2 L_2^2$ — only the $L_1 L_2$ part of the cross-term vanishes; the $m_2 L_2^2$ piece survives because it comes from link 2's own rotation, which is geometry-independent. The cleanest decoupling is at the limit $L_1 \to 0$, not at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$. This is exactly the inertia matrix you will see again in Module 3, and it is the launchpad for writing Coriolis and centrifugal terms via the Christoffel symbols of $M(q)$.

That angle is exactly $\\theta_2$ (after the cosine-difference simplification).\nWhy is $T$ quadratic in $\\dot\\theta_i$? Velocities are linear in $\\dot\\theta_i$ (chain rule), so $v^2$ is quadratic — always, for any holonomic system with stationary constraints.\nWhy does $V$ have no rate dependence? Gravitational potential is a function of position only; it knows nothing about how fast the system is moving.\nWhy $L = T - V$ and not $T + V$? This is the Hamilton's-principle choice that makes the Euler–Lagrange equations reproduce Newton's second law. It is a convention by construction, not derivable from it.\n\nMISCONCEPTIONS & GOTCHAS\n- Writing the rotation block of $T_2$ with just $\\theta_2$ instead of $\\theta_1+\\theta_2$. Wrong: link 2's world orientation is cumulative. The relative angle $\\theta_2$ shows up locally in the joint-to-joint transform; the absolute angle is the sum.\n- Forgetting the $(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)$ factor on $L_2\\sin/\\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)$ when differentiating. The chain rule demands it — the second link's angular rate in the world is $\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2$, not $\\dot\\theta_2$.\n- Dropping or mis-signing the cross-term $2 L_1 L_2 \\cos\\theta_2\\,\\dot\\theta_1(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)$ when expanding $v_2^2$. Forgetting it leaves the arm artificially decoupled; getting its sign wrong inverts the coupling.\n- Misapplying the identity: $\\sin\\alpha\\sin\\beta + \\cos\\alpha\\cos\\beta = \\cos(\\alpha-\\beta)$, NOT $\\cos(\\alpha+\\beta)$. With $\\alpha = \\theta_1$ and $\\beta = \\theta_1+\\theta_2$, $\\alpha - \\beta = -\\theta_2$, and the result is $\\cos(-\\theta_2) = \\cos\\theta_2$.\n- Putting $\\theta_1$ inside $V$ when the mass is at the end of a horizontal rod and you forget that height is $L_1\\sin\\theta_1$, not $L_1\\cos\\theta_1$. Here $\\theta_1$ is measured f\n\n── PAGE TEXT (what the student is reading) ──\nLecture 03 · Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm Lecture 03 · Module 2 · Robotics Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm From transformation matrices to the Lagrangian — a fully worked tip-mass derivation. Today we walk through, step by careful step, how a 2-link planar arm with tip masses goes from geometry to Lagrangian. We start with homogeneous transformation matrices, read off the tip positions, differentiate to get velocities, square them, and stitch everything together into kinetic and potential energy. By the end you will have $L = T - V$ written out explicitly — exactly the form Module 3 will need when we feed it into the Euler–Lagrange equations. Contents 0 What this lecture covers 1 Transformation matrices 2 Tip positions 3 Velocities by chain rule 4 Square and simplify 5 Kinetic energy $T$ 6 Potential energy $V$ 7 The Lagrangian $L = T - V$ · Concepts in play · Practice — try on your own § 0 What this lecture covers We take a 2-link planar robot arm with point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ at the distal end of each link, and derive — from scratch — its kinematics and energies. The destination is the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, written in terms of the joint angles $\\theta_1, \\theta_2$ and their rates $\\dot\\theta_1, \\dot\\theta_2$. Along the way we'll touch every tool you need: homogeneous transformations, the chain rule on position, the trig identity $\\sin\\alpha\\sin\\beta + \\cos\\alpha\\cos\\beta = \\cos(\\alpha - \\beta)$, and the usual gravity potential. This is the setup we will hand to the Euler–Lagrange machinery in Module 3. Don't skim the algebra in step 4 — the $\\cos\\theta_2$ cross-term is the whole reason this problem is interesting. Setup The system on the table Link lengths $L_1, L_2$; joint angles $\\theta_1$ (link 1 from horizontal) and $\\theta_2$ (link 2 from link 1); tip masses $m_1, m_2$; gravity $g$ acts in $-y$. § 1 Write the transformation matrices for each link We use 2D homogeneous transformations so rotation and translation live in one matrix. From the base to the tip of link 1: $T_1 = \\begin{bmatrix} \\cos\\theta_1 & -\\sin\\theta_1 & L_1\\cos\\theta_1 \\\\ \\sin\\theta_1 & \\cos\\theta_1 & L_1\\sin\\theta_1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\end{bmatrix}$ From the base to the tip of link 2 (i.e. the location of $m_2$): $T_2 = \\begin{bmatrix} \\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) & -\\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) & L_1\\cos\\theta_1 + L_2\\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) \\\\ \\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) & \\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) & L_1\\sin\\theta_1 + L_2\\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\end{bmatrix}$ Notice that the rotation block of $T_2$ uses the sum $\\theta_1 + \\theta_2$ — link 2's orientation in the world is the cumulative rotation, not just $\\theta_2$. Why homogeneous? One matrix for rotation and translation The third row/column lets us compose rotations and translations by simple matrix multiplication — $T_2$ is literally $T_1$ composed with link 2's local transform. Interactive · pick Pick the rotation entry for $T_2$ Now you pick the (1,1) entry of $T_2$ yourself. The point is to convince you that link 2's world-frame orientation is the cumulative rotation $\\theta_1+\\theta_2$, not just $\\theta_2$ — and certainly not just $\\theta_1$. § 2 Read off the tip positions The right-hand column of each transformation matrix is the position of that link's tip in world coordinates. For $m_1$ (end of link 1): $\\begin{aligned} x_1 &= L_1\\cos\\theta_1 \\\\ y_1 &= L_1\\sin\\theta_1 \\end{aligned}$ For $m_2$ (end of link 2): $\\begin{aligned} x_2 &= L_1\\cos\\theta_1 + L_2\\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) \\\\ y_2 &= L_1\\sin\\theta_1 + L_2\\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) \\end{aligned}$ This is just forward kinematics — geometry, no dynamics yet. Interactive · animator Animated forward kinematics · scrub the joints, watch the tip positions Now you drag $\\theta_1$ and $\\theta_2$ and watch the tip-position formulas update live. The point is to see — not just read — that $x_2$ accumulates a contribution from both links, while $x_1$ depends only on $\\theta_1$. § 3 Differentiate to get velocities Apply the chain rule — $\\theta_1$ and $\\theta_2$ are functions of time, so $\\cos\\theta_1$ differentiates to $-\\sin\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1$, and $\\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)$ picks up the factor $(\\dot\\theta_1 + \\dot\\theta_2)$. For $m_1$: $\\begin{aligned} \\dot x_1 &= -L_1\\sin\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1 \\\\ \\dot y_1 &= L_1\\cos\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1 \\end{aligned}$ For $m_2$: $\\begin{aligned} \\dot x_2 &= -L_1\\sin\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1 - L_2\\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)\\,(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2) \\\\ \\dot y_2 &= L_1\\cos\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1 + L_2\\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)\\,(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2) \\end{aligned}$ The $(\\dot\\theta_1 + \\dot\\theta_2)$ factor on the second term is the easiest thing to forget — link 2's angular rate in the world frame is the sum of both joint rates. Interactive · builder Build $\\dot x_2$ term by term Now you build $\\dot x_2$ yourself by dragging chain-rule pieces onto a blank expression. You'll discover the hard way that the second term picks up the factor $(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)$, not just $\\dot\\theta_2$ — the single most common slip in this derivation. § 4 Square and simplify: $v^2$ for each mass For $m_1$ the algebra is short — Pythagoras plus $\\sin^2 + \\cos^2 = 1$: $v_1^2 = \\dot x_1^2 + \\dot y_1^2 = L_1^2\\dot\\theta_1^2(\\sin^2\\theta_1 + \\cos^2\\theta_1) = L_1^2\\dot\\theta_1^2$ For $m_2$ the algebra is longer. Square both $\\dot x_2$ and $\\dot y_2$ and add: $\\begin{aligned} v_2^2 =\\;& L_1^2\\sin^2\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\\sin^2(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)^2 \\\\ & + 2L_1L_2\\sin\\theta_1\\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)\\,\\dot\\theta_1(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2) \\\\ & + L_1^2\\cos^2\\theta_1\\,\\dot\\theta_1^2 + L_2^2\\cos^2(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)^2 \\\\ & + 2L_1L_2\\cos\\theta_1\\cos(\\theta_1+\\theta_2)\\,\\dot\\theta_1(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2) \\end{aligned}$ Now collapse using two identities: $\\sin^2\\alpha + \\cos^2\\alpha = 1$ $\\sin\\alpha\\sin\\beta + \\cos\\alpha\\cos\\beta = \\cos(\\alpha-\\beta)$ with $\\alpha = \\theta_1$ and $\\beta = \\theta_1+\\theta_2$, so $\\alpha - \\beta = -\\theta_2$ and $\\cos(-\\theta_2) = \\cos\\theta_2$: $\\boxed{\\,v_2^2 = L_1^2\\dot\\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\\cos\\theta_2\\,\\dot\\theta_1(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)\\,}$ That $\\cos\\theta_2$ cross-term is the coupling between the two joints — it's what makes a 2-link arm a genuinely nonlinear system. Identity in play Keep this on the tip of your tongue $\\sin\\alpha\\sin\\beta + \\cos\\alpha\\cos\\beta = \\cos(\\alpha-\\beta)$. It shows up every time you square the velocity of a multi-link chain. Interactive · derive Collapse the cross terms · derive the $\\cos\\theta_2$ coupling Now you derive the boxed result for $v_2^2$ yourself by choosing which identity to apply at each step. The four cross-products in the expansion collapse into a single $\\cos\\theta_2$ term — and you'll see exactly which trig identity makes that happen. § 5 Assemble the kinetic energy $T$ With both squared speeds in hand, kinetic energy is just $T = \\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \\tfrac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2$: $T = \\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2\\dot\\theta_1^2 + \\tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \\left[ L_1^2\\dot\\theta_1^2 + L_2^2(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)^2 + 2L_1L_2\\cos\\theta_2\\,\\dot\\theta_1(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2) \\right]$ The shape to notice: $T$ is quadratic in the joint rates $\\dot\\theta_i$, with coefficients that depend on $\\theta_2$ alone (not $\\theta_1$). That's a hint of the inertia matrix $M(q)$ — but we'll meet that properly in Module 3. Looking ahead The manipulator form is hiding in here Group the $\\dot\\theta_i\\dot\\theta_j$ coefficients and you'll have $T = \\tfrac{1}{2}\\dot q^\\top M(q)\\,\\dot q$ — the standard manipulator form. Interactive · animator Animated coupling · watch $\\cos\\theta_2$ shape the kinetic energy Now you scrub $\\theta_2$ and watch the three contributions to $T$ (the pure-$\\dot\\theta_1$ piece, the pure-$(\\dot\\theta_1+\\dot\\theta_2)$ piece, and the $\\cos\\theta_2$ cross-term) shrink, swap, and vanish. The point is to feel where the coupling matters and where it disappears. § 6 Potential energy $V$ With $y$ increasing upward and gravity $g$ acting in $-y$, each mass contributes $m_i g y_i$: $V = m_1 g y_1 + m_2 g y_2$ Substitute the tip-position formulas from step 2: $V = m_1 g L_1 \\sin\\theta_1 + m_2 g \\left[ L_1\\sin\\theta_1 + L_2\\sin(\\theta_1+\\theta_2) \\right]$ Notice $V$ depends only on the configuration $(\\theta_1, \\theta_2)$ — never on the rates. That's a defining feature of conservative potentials. § 7 The Lagrangian $L = T - V$ Stitching it together: $L = T - V$ $\\begin{aligned} L =\\;& \\tfrac{1}{2} m_1 L_1^2 \\dot\\theta_1^2 \\\\ & + \\tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \\left[ L_1^2 \\dot\\theta_1^2 + L_2^2 (\\dot\\theta_1 + \\dot\\theta_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \\cos\\theta_2 \\, \\dot\\theta_1 (\\dot\\theta_1 + \\dot\\theta_2) \\right] \\\\ & - m_1 g L_1 \\sin\\theta_1 - m_2 g \\left[ L_1 \\sin\\theta_1 + L_2 \\sin(\\theta_1 + \\theta_2) \\right] \\end{aligned}$ This is the object Module 3 will plug into the Euler–Lagrange equations : $\\frac{d}{dt}\\frac{\\partial L","contextLabel":"Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm","openingLine":"I'm reading Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm. Lecture 03 · Module 2 · Robotics

Kinematics and energies for a 2-link planar robot arm

From transformation matrices to the Lagrangian — a fully worked tip-mass derivation.

Today we walk through, step by careful step, how a 2-link planar arm with tip masses goes from geometry to Lagrangian. We start with homogeneous transformation matrices, read off the tip positions, differentiate to get velocities, square them, and stitch everything together into kinetic and potential energy.

By the end you will have $L = T - V$ written out explicitly — exactly the form Module 3 will need when we feed it into the Euler–Lagrange equations.

  4. 3Velocities by chain rule
